question.:question/problem: Given that $f(x)=\frac{1}{{x}^{5/3}}$ and that ${F}^{'}(x)=f(x)$, calculate $F(x).$ Assume $x>0$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Remember that integration is the opposite of differentiation. So, if ${F}^{'}(x)=f(x),$ then integrating both sides of this equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{'}(x) & =f(x) \\ \int {F}^{'}(x)\,\text{d}x & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x \\ F(x) & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $\frac{1}{{x}^{5/3}}={x}^{-5/3}.$ So, we can use the power rule with $n=-\frac{5}{3}$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x) & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {x}^{-5/3}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{-5/3+1}}{(-\frac{5}{3}+1)}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{-2/3}}{\left(-\frac{2}{3}\right)}+C \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}{x}^{-2/3}+C \\  & =-\frac{3}{2{x}^{2/3}}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: If a curve $C$ is given by $y=(e^{x})\cdot (x)$, calculate the slope of the tangent line to the curve at the point where $x=0$.
question.:question/worked-solution:
We differentiate using the product rule. Let $u(x)=e^{x}$ and $v(x)=x.$ Then, we have

$$
u'(x)=e^{x},\quad v'(x)=1.
$$

Applying the product rule gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx} &=uv'(x)+vu'(x) \\ &=(e^{x})\cdot (1)+(x)\cdot (e^{x}) \\ &=\left(x + 1\right) e^{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the slope of the tangent line, we now substitute $x=0$ into the formula and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\left.\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}\right|_{x=0} &=\begin{aligned}&(e^{(0)})\cdot (1) \\ &{}+((0))\cdot (e^{(0)})\end{aligned} \\ &=(1)\cdot (1)+(0)\cdot (1) \\ &=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent line is $1.$

question.:question/worked-solution:
We differentiate using the product rule. Let $u(x)=x - 1$ and $v(x)=\ln{\left(x \right)}.$ Then, we have

$$
u'(x)=1,\quad v'(x)=\frac{1}{x}.
$$

Applying the product rule gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx} &=uv'(x)+vu'(x) \\ &=(x - 1)\cdot \left(\frac{1}{x}\right)+(\ln{\left(x \right)})\cdot (1) \\ &=\frac{x - 1}{x}+(1)\cdot (\ln{\left(x \right)}).\end{aligned}
$$

To find the slope of the tangent line, we now substitute $x=e^{2}$ into the formula and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\left.\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}\right|_{x=e^{2}} &=\begin{aligned}&((e^{2}) - 1)\cdot \left(\frac{1}{(e^{2})}\right) \\ &{}+(\ln{\left((e^{2}) \right)})\cdot (1)\end{aligned} \\ &=(-1 + e^{2})\cdot (e^{-2})+(2)\cdot (1) \\ &=3 - e^{-2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent line is $3 - e^{-2}.$

question.:question/problem: Given that $f(x,y)$ varies with both $x$ and $y,$ which of the following **cannot** be the slope field for the differential equation $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=f(x,y)?$

$$

question.:question/problem: If $\cos x=-\frac{7}{9},$ then $\cos (x+16\pi )=$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The period of $y=\cos x$ is $2\pi .$ Therefore, for an integer $n$ we have

$$
\cos x=\cos (x+2n\pi ).
$$

Substituting $n=8$ into the right-hand-side of the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\cos x &=\cos (x+2\cdot 8\cdot \pi )=\cos (x+16\pi ).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, if $\cos x=-\frac{7}{9},$ then $\cos (x+16\pi )=-\frac{7}{9}.$

$$

Substituting $n=7$ into the right-hand-side of the above gives

\begin{aligned}\cos x &=\cos (x+2\cdot 7\cdot \pi )=\cos (x+14\pi ).\end{aligned}

$$

$$
